svg.title: Stress, fatigue, dehydration and airsickness
svg.desc: A two by two table. Columns are stress and fatigue. Rows are acute, short term, and chronic, long term. Acute stress is an immediate perceived threat that a healthy person copes with; chronic stress is a burden beyond coping, so see a physician. Acute fatigue is cured by rest and 8 hours of sleep; chronic fatigue is not relieved by rest, so see a physician. Two cards below cover dehydration and heatstroke, and airsickness.
svg.text: Stress, fatigue, dehydration and airsickness
Four things that can make a healthy pilot unsafe. Stress and fatigue each come in a short-term and a
long-term kind, and the two kinds need different fixes.
Stress
Fatigue
Acute: short term
Immediate threat seen as danger: the fight or flight
response, real or imagined. A healthy person normally
copes.
Acute: short term
Tiredness after strenuous effort, excitement or lack
of sleep. Rest and 8 hours of sound sleep ordinarily
cure it. If acutely tired, stay on the ground.
Chronic: long term
A burden beyond your ability to cope; performance
falls sharply. Not safe to fly. See a physician.
Chronic: long term
Long period, usually psychological roots. Diet, rest
and sleep do not relieve it. See a physician.
Stressors: physical (noise, vibration), physiological (fatigue), psychological (difficult work or personal
situations). Stress releases adrenaline and raises heart rate, respiration and blood pressure.
Dehydration and heatstroke
Causes: hot flight decks and flight lines, wind,
humidity, and diuretic drinks (coffee, tea,
alcohol, caffeinated soft drinks).
Signs: headache, fatigue, cramps, sleepiness,
dizziness.
Thirst comes late, at about a 1.5 quart deficit (2
percent of body weight). Do not wait for it.
Drink two to four quarts of water every 24 hours,
as a guide.
Heatstroke: the body cannot control its
temperature. It may show only as a collapse. Drink
one pint per hour in moderate heat stress, one
quart in severe.
Airsickness
The brain gets conflicting messages about the state
of the body.
Symptoms: general discomfort, nausea, dizziness,
paleness, sweating, vomiting.
It usually goes away within the first few lessons.
It says nothing about your ability.
Tell your instructor. Open the fresh air vents,
look at objects outside, avoid unnecessary head
movements.
Dramamine-type medicine is not recommended while
flying: drowsiness and other problems.
